title: Toimiko auto huollon jälkeen?
subtitle: Did the car work after the service?

blocks.text: Every dialogue since Lesson 3 has quietly used a question ending you've never had named: toimiko, suositteletko, ilmenikö. It's one tiny suffix doing all that work. This lesson makes it explicit, so you can build your own yes/no questions instead of only recognising ones already written for you.

blocks.translation: Did the car work after the service?

blocks.title: No 'do/does/did' needed
blocks.text: English builds yes/no questions with a helper verb: 'did it work?', 'do you recommend?'. Finnish needs no helper verb at all — it just clips a small particle onto the main verb itself and moves that verb to the front. One word does the whole job that three English words do.
Piece 1 — -ko/-kö attaches to the verb, verb moves first

blocks.content: To turn a statement into a yes/no question, take the main verb, move it to the front of the sentence, and attach {-ko|grammar|question particle|question marker} (or -kö after front vowels). Toimi (worked) → {Toimiko|grammar|question particle -ko|did it work?} auto? Suosittelet (you recommend) → {Suositteletko|grammar|question particle -ko|do you recommend?} tätä?

items.fi: {Toimiko|grammar|question particle -ko|did it work} auto huollon jälkeen?
items.en: Did the car work after the service?
Do you recommend this repair shop?

blocks.text: Piece 2 — -ko/-kö also attaches to other words, for emphasis

blocks.title: Not just verbs
blocks.text: The same particle can attach to nouns or other words when the question is really about that word specifically, not the action. Onko sinulla autoa? — 'do you have a car?' — the particle rides on on because the yes/no hinges on having, not on some other part of the sentence. Whatever word the question truly turns on is the word that gets -ko/-kö.

items.en: Do you have a car being repaired?

blocks.text: Piece 3 — Answering: kyllä/ei, or just repeat the verb

blocks.content: You already have kyllä (yes, Lesson 1) and ei (no/doesn't, Lesson 3). But the most natural Finnish answer often just echoes the verb from the question, positively or negatively: Suositteletko? — Suosittelen. (Do you recommend? — I recommend [i.e. yes].) Toimiko? — Ei toiminut. (Did it work? — It didn't work [i.e. no].)

items.en: Do you recommend it? — I recommend it (yes).
Did the car work? — It didn't work (no).

lines.speaker: A
lines.en: Did the car work after the service?

lines.speaker: B
lines.fi: Ei toiminut. Ilmenikö sinulla samanlaisia ongelmia?
lines.en: It didn't work. Did you have similar problems?

lines.speaker: A
lines.en: Does the repair shop have a good reputation otherwise?

lines.speaker: B
lines.en: Not very good. I'd recommend a different one.

blocks.title: Paul Noble Rule
blocks.text: Go back to Lesson 3's dialogue right now: Toimiko auto huollon jälkeen? was sitting there the whole time. You've been reading -ko/-kö questions since your third lesson without a name for them. That's the entire Paul Noble method in miniature — recognise first, name later, and the naming barely changes anything because you already knew how to use it.

blocks.content: Toimiko: TOI-mi-ko (three syllables, rising slightly in question intonation at the end, like English). Suositteletko: SUO-sit-te-let-ko (long word — the -ko lands light and quick at the very end). Onko: ON-ko (short, crisp, very common).

rows.en: question particle, attaches to the fronted verb (or key word)

blocks.title: What you now own
items: the -ko/-kö question particle, attached to a fronted verb: toimiko, suositteletko, onko
the same particle attaching to other key words for a more targeted question
the natural way to answer: echo the verb (suosittelen) instead of always saying kyllä/ei
you can now build your own yes/no questions instead of just recognising them
you can look back at every earlier dialogue and see this particle you'd been reading all along
